sources.title: Gunter Last and Mathew Penrose, Lectures on the Poisson Process, author-hosted 2017 version
sources.locator: Complete focused ranges inspected: Chapter 1 §§1.1–1.4 and Poisson mass/moment formulas, PDF pp.13–18; Chapter 2 §§2.1–2.4, pp.21–29; Chapter 3 §§3.1–3.3 through Theorem 3.9, pp.31–37; Chapter 4 §§4.1–4.4 through Proposition 4.12, pp.38–48; Chapter 13 §§13.1–13.4 through Theorem 13.11, pp.139–145. The named results in these ranges are individually dispositioned below.

contents.name: Poisson mass formula, probability generating function, factorial moments, and variance (equations 1.4–1.11)
Proposition 1.1: scalar Poisson size-bias recursion
contents.reason: The converse proof derives the finite-vector count recursion locally; no scalar uniqueness argument is imported without that proof.

contents.name: Proposition 1.2: sums of independent Poisson variables and conditional binomial splitting
Proposition 1.3: independent thinning of a Poisson variable
contents.reason: Thinning is a separate transformation theorem and the assigned pair contains no retained/deleted-point marking construction.

contents.name: Proposition 1.4: Poisson limit theorem for rare independent summands
contents.reason: This asymptotic approximation theorem is outside the exact finite and locally finite process laws claimed on the assigned pages.

contents.name: Proposition 1.5: Gamma–Poisson mixture gives a negative-binomial law
contents.reason: The Cox example uses a two-point directing distribution; no Gamma mixing or negative-binomial result is claimed.

contents.name: Definition 2.1: point process as a measurable random counting measure
Example 2.2: one-point process as a random Dirac measure
contents.reason: The local definition permits finite sums of Dirac masses and the empty configuration.

contents.name: Example 2.3: finite binomial process
contents.reason: The finite Poisson construction uses product-distributed locations conditional on a Poisson total.

contents.name: Definition 2.4: proper point process
contents.reason: The chosen configuration space is defined from countable sums of Dirac masses, so properness is built into this page’s point-process domain.

contents.name: Definition 2.5: expected intensity measure
Example 2.6: intensity of a binomial process
contents.reason: The example computes a binomial-process mean measure, while the assigned B page compares Poisson and Cox laws instead.

contents.name: Proposition 2.7: Campbell formula
Definition 2.8: Laplace functional of a point process
contents.reason: The A theorem states and proves the Poisson Laplace formula using this nonnegative-integral convention.

contents.name: Example 2.9: Laplace functional of the binomial process
contents.reason: A binomial-process transform is not required for the Poisson/Cox formulas or the finite-window variance comparison.

contents.name: Proposition 2.10: finite-dimensional counts and law characterization, including the Laplace-functional equivalences
contents.reason: The local item proves the count-cylinder implication; the source’s Laplace-transform uniqueness equivalences are not imported.

contents.name: Definition 2.11: locally finite measures on metric spaces via bounded sets
contents.reason: The source uses a metric bounded-set convention; this pair instead states local finiteness on compact sets in an LCH second-countable space.

contents.name: Proposition 2.12: compactly supported Laplace functionals determine a metric-space process law
contents.reason: The bounded-support metric characterization is not needed for the independent-count and configuration-cylinder proofs here.

contents.name: Definition 2.13: locally finite point process
contents.reason: The local definition states locally finite counting-measure realizations on the assigned LCH space.

contents.name: Proposition 2.14: continuous compactly supported test functions determine process law
contents.reason: No vague-topology or continuous-test-function law characterization is stated on the assigned pages.

contents.name: Definition 3.1: Poisson process by independent counts and Poisson marginals
Proposition 3.2: uniqueness in distribution for a fixed Poisson intensity
contents.reason: The independent-count definition supplies identical finite count laws, and the local cylinder lemma supplies the law conclusion.

contents.name: Theorem 3.3: independent superposition of Poisson processes
contents.reason: The general construction proves countable superposition by independent finite-cell processes and verifies the count laws directly.

contents.name: Definition 3.4: mixed-binomial process
contents.reason: The finite-intensity theorem gives the explicit mixed-binomial construction.

contents.name: Proposition 3.5: Poisson law of a Poisson-mixed binomial process
Theorem 3.6: existence on a finite or sigma-finite intensity space
Corollary 3.7: proper version of a Poisson process on an arbitrary measurable space
contents.reason: The local domain uses countable Dirac sums, while the arbitrary-measurable-space representation claim is not needed.

contents.name: Proposition 3.8: finite-intensity mixed-binomial representation and conditional location law
Theorem 3.9: Poisson characterization by an if-and-only-if Laplace-functional formula
contents.reason: The forward Laplace formula is proved locally, but the source theorem also claims a converse requiring a separate transform-uniqueness argument not included in this pair.

contents.name: Theorem 4.1: add-one Mecke equation and its converse
Lemma 4.2: recursion for factorial measures
contents.reason: This factorial-measure recursion is a prerequisite for the planned second-order spatial summaries and is outside the first-order Mecke scope here.

contents.name: Proposition 4.3: existence and measurability of factorial measures
contents.reason: Factorial measures are used by the planned Palm and spatial-summary page, not by this pair’s first-order identities.

contents.name: Theorem 4.4: multivariate Mecke equation
contents.reason: The multi-insertion formula is a Palm/factorial-measure result beyond the single-point Mecke identity proved here.

contents.name: Theorem 4.5: multivariate deletion Mecke formula
contents.reason: The multi-point deletion formula depends on factorial measures and is reserved for the planned Palm-law development.

contents.name: Definition 4.6: Janossy measures
contents.reason: Janossy measures support finite-window point-pattern likelihoods, which are assigned to the later likelihood page.

contents.name: Theorem 4.7: Janossy measures determine a finite-window restriction law
contents.reason: This finite-window distribution reconstruction belongs with the planned point-pattern likelihood treatment.

contents.name: Example 4.8: Janossy measures of a finite-window Poisson process
contents.reason: The example computes finite-window pattern densities and is reserved for the later likelihood page.

contents.name: Definition 4.9: factorial moment measure
contents.reason: The factorial-moment measure is a planned second-order spatial summary, outside the first-order point-process formulas here.

contents.name: Corollary 4.10: factorial moment measure of a Poisson process
contents.reason: The tensor-power factorial-measure identity supports later pair summaries and is not needed for the scalar moment identities here.

contents.name: Lemma 4.11: factorial-moment expansion under exponential growth bounds
contents.reason: The expansion requires factorial-moment growth hypotheses and analytic series control that are not part of the assigned claims.

contents.name: Proposition 4.12: factorial moment measures determine process law under growth bounds
contents.reason: This moment-determinacy theorem has additional growth and analytic hypotheses absent from the assigned first-order theory.

contents.name: Definition 13.1: random measure as a measurable measure-valued map
Proposition 13.2: random-measure law characterization by finite-dimensional laws and Laplace functionals
contents.reason: The page uses count-cylinder uniqueness only; a full random-measure Laplace-transform equivalence would require a separate analytic uniqueness proof.

contents.name: Example 13.3: random field induces a random intensity measure
contents.reason: Random-field measurability and density construction are not required for the supplied-kernel Cox definition or finite-window example.

contents.name: Lemma 13.4: measurability of the Poisson law as a function of its intensity
contents.reason: The Cox definition deliberately supplies a regular conditional kernel and makes no claim that a canonical measurable Poisson-law kernel exists.

contents.name: Definition 13.5: Cox process as conditionally Poisson given a random measure
Proposition 13.6: Cox random-integral second moment and variance equivalence
Theorem 13.7: a Cox law determines the directing-measure law
contents.reason: The source’s converse invokes an external analytic uniqueness result (Appendix B, Proposition B.5), which is expressly excluded from this page.

contents.name: Theorem 13.8: Mecke-type characterization of Cox processes
contents.reason: This conditional Cox-Mecke characterization is beyond the assigned Poisson Mecke converse and would require separate conditional-kernel hypotheses.

contents.name: Lemma 13.9: locally finite and diffuse measure spaces are measurable subsets
contents.reason: The assigned model directly equips locally finite measures with evaluation sigma-algebra and makes no diffuse-subspace measurability claim.

contents.name: Definition 13.10: locally finite and diffuse random measures
contents.reason: The local definition includes locally finite random measures; no diffuse assumption or conclusion is imported.

contents.name: Theorem 13.11: diffuse directing measures are determined by one-dimensional marginals
contents.reason: Its proof uses unreviewed Chapter 6 results on simplicity and Cox identifiability; the owner direction expressly excludes this claim.

contents.name: Exercises 1.1–1.11
contents.reason: These exercises pose additional scalar, transform, factorial-measure, or Palm problems beyond the named claims and proofs assigned to this pair.

contents.name: Exercises 2.1–2.9
contents.reason: These exercises pose additional scalar, transform, factorial-measure, or Palm problems beyond the named claims and proofs assigned to this pair.

contents.name: Exercises 3.1–3.9
contents.reason: These exercises pose additional scalar, transform, factorial-measure, or Palm problems beyond the named claims and proofs assigned to this pair.

contents.name: Exercises 4.1–4.7
contents.reason: These exercises pose additional scalar, transform, factorial-measure, or Palm problems beyond the named claims and proofs assigned to this pair.

sources.title: Adrian Baddeley, Spatial Point Processes and their Applications, complete lecture notes
sources.locator: Complete Lecture 1, PDF pp.1–25, including Definitions 1.1–1.9, Lemma 1.1, Theorems 1.1–1.3 and their numbered corollaries/examples; the finite-window conditional-property proof and introductory definitions were inspected in full.

contents.name: Definition 1.1: one-dimensional homogeneous Poisson process
contents.reason: The time-interval specialization and interarrival-time consequences are not needed for the spatial locally finite Borel-space contract.

contents.name: Definition 1.2: homogeneous spatial Poisson process in the plane
contents.reason: The general independent-count definition includes this special case without restricting the space to the plane.

contents.name: Lemma 1.1: conditional binomial property in a finite window
contents.reason: The local mixed-binomial proof gives the conditional product-location construction and its multinomial count split.

contents.name: Definition 1.3: Poisson process on a general spatial space
contents.reason: The local definition uses the independent-count contract but does not import the source’s diffuse-intensity/no-atom restriction.

contents.name: Example 1.1: uniform Poisson process in three dimensions
contents.reason: The three-dimensional homogeneous example is not used by the abstract finite-window comparison.

contents.name: Example 1.2: inhomogeneous planar Poisson process
contents.reason: No spatial intensity-density example is needed to establish the locally finite measure-based statements.

contents.name: Example 1.3: uniform Poisson process on the sphere
contents.reason: The spherical area-measure example is outside the assigned finite-window count comparison.

contents.name: Definition 1.4: canonical configuration space and its evaluation sigma-field
contents.reason: The local definition equips locally finite counting measures with the sigma-algebra generated by all Borel evaluations.

contents.name: Definition 1.5: distribution of a point process
Definition 1.6: finite-dimensional count distributions
Theorem 1.1: finite-dimensional count laws determine process law
Corollary 1.1: independent Poisson count axioms characterize a Poisson process
contents.reason: This is exactly the independent-count definition used on the local A page.

contents.name: Theorem 1.2: capacity functionals determine simple-process laws
contents.reason: The result is restricted to simple point processes, while the assigned theory explicitly allows multiplicities.

contents.name: Corollary 1.2: capacity characterization of a uniform Poisson process
contents.reason: The simple-process capacity criterion is not needed for the independent-count or Laplace proofs.

contents.name: Corollary 1.3: capacity characterization of a binomial process
contents.reason: The binomial-process capacity formula is outside the finite Poisson/Cox comparison assigned here.

contents.name: Definition 1.7: stationary point process
contents.reason: Stationarity and translation invariance are reserved for later spatial-summary topics, not the assigned models.

contents.name: Lemma 1.2: stationarity characterized by the capacity functional
contents.reason: This translation-invariance result depends on stationarity and capacity functionals, neither of which is in scope.

contents.name: Definition 1.8: marked point process
contents.reason: Mark spaces and projected marked configurations are not included in the assigned Poisson/Cox point-process scope.

contents.name: Example 1.4: unbounded marks can violate local finiteness after projection
contents.reason: The warning concerns mark projection, which is not a construction or claim on either assigned page.

contents.name: Example 1.5: a bounded mark slab projects to a planar Poisson process
contents.reason: Independent marking and projection are excluded from the assigned example and definitions.

contents.name: Theorem 1.3: independent marking equivalence for Poisson processes
contents.reason: The marking theorem requires mark-space product structure and is not proved or claimed in this pair.

contents.name: Definition 1.9: contact distance to the nearest point
contents.reason: Nearest-neighbor spatial summaries are planned for the later spatial-summary page, not this foundational pair.

sources.title: The Stacks Project, Section 5.13: Locally quasi-compact spaces, Tag 08ZQ
sources.locator: Lemma 5.13.2 and its complete proof: compact neighborhoods can be shrunk inside an open neighborhood in a locally compact Hausdorff space; the second-countable compact-exhaustion sequence is proved locally.

contents.name: Lemma 5.13.2: shrinking compact neighborhoods inside open sets
contents.reason: This source supplies the local shrinking step; the countable basis, finite-union compactness, and cofinal exhaustion are proved in the new item.
